title: Linezolid: Serotonin, CBC, and Neuropathy Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Linezolid treats selected serious gram-positive infections but acts as a reversible monoamine-oxidase inhibitor. Monitor CBC, serotonergic interactions, blood pressure risk from adrenergic/tyramine exposure, and visual or peripheral neuropathy with longer treatment.
recognize: Thrombocytopenia or other myelosuppression may develop, especially with prolonged therapy or organ dysfunction.
Agitation, clonus, hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, tremor, rigidity, fever, or autonomic instability can indicate serotonin syndrome.
Visual changes or peripheral neuropathy are more concerning with extended treatment.
priorities: Reconcile serotonergic and adrenergic medications before administration.
Trend CBC as ordered and report bleeding, bruising, pallor, or infection findings.
Escalate serotonin-syndrome findings or new visual symptoms promptly.
assessMonitor: CBC, neurologic findings, vision symptoms, BP, glucose in susceptible patients, sodium when clinically indicated, and infection response.
interventions: Coordinate medication-interaction review rather than independently stopping essential psychiatric therapy.
Reinforce avoidance of excessive high-tyramine foods when instructed by the treatment plan.
medicationSafety: Linezolid is contraindicated with MAO inhibitors or within the specified washout interval in the label.
Serotonergic drugs can increase serotonin-syndrome risk.
Longer courses increase neuropathy risk.
teaching: Report unusual bruising, severe diarrhea, visual change, numbness/tingling, agitation, tremor, or fever.
Bring a complete medication list, including antidepressants and OTC products.
delegationScope: Medication administration follows state/facility LPN/LVN policy; assessment of toxicity or interaction syndromes requires licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Treating linezolid like an ordinary antibiotic and missing its MAOI-related interaction profile.
oneLinePearl: Linezolid = antibiotic plus MAOI-style interaction thinking.

title: Isoniazid: Hepatitis and Neuropathy Monitoring
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Isoniazid is a key tuberculosis drug with a boxed warning for severe hepatitis. Monitor for hepatic symptoms and peripheral neuropathy; pyridoxine supplementation is used for patients at increased neuropathy risk according to the TB regimen.
recognize: Anorexia, persistent nausea/vomiting, fatigue, malaise, weakness, dark urine, or jaundice can indicate hepatitis.
Numbness, tingling, or burning in the extremities can signal peripheral neuropathy.
priorities: Review liver risk factors and alcohol use.
Report symptoms of hepatitis immediately rather than waiting for routine laboratory follow-up.
Reinforce adherence to the complete multidrug TB regimen when treating active disease.
assessMonitor: Clinical hepatitis symptoms, liver tests when ordered, neuropathy symptoms, medication adherence, and interacting anticonvulsant levels when relevant.
interventions: Administer pyridoxine when ordered for higher-risk patients.
Coordinate directly observed therapy/public-health follow-up when part of the local TB plan.
medicationSafety: Alcohol increases hepatotoxicity risk.
Isoniazid can alter metabolism of other medications; interaction review is required.
redFlags: Severe persistent GI symptoms with malaise
teaching: Avoid alcohol and report hepatitis symptoms promptly.
Do not stop one TB drug independently while continuing the others without TB-team direction.
delegationScope: TB medication administration may be supervised under public-health protocols; toxicity assessment and changes to the regimen require licensed/provider escalation.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient with anorexia and dark urine that mild GI upset is expected.
oneLinePearl: Isoniazid: think liver first, nerves second, adherence always.

title: Rifampin: Interactions and Orange Secretions
bottomLine: Rifampin is a potent enzyme inducer with many clinically important drug interactions. Orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, saliva, and tears can be expected, but hepatitis, severe rash, cytopenias, or major interaction effects are not.
recognize: Body-fluid discoloration can permanently stain soft contact lenses.
Reduced effectiveness of interacting medications can occur because rifampin accelerates metabolism of many drugs.
priorities: Perform full medication reconciliation before and during therapy.
Monitor for hepatitis symptoms and treatment response.
Reinforce multidrug adherence for active TB.
assessMonitor: Liver symptoms/tests when ordered, CBC when indicated, adherence, contraceptive reliability, anticoagulant or transplant-drug effects, and TB symptoms.
interventions: Coordinate alternative or backup contraception when enzyme induction may reduce hormonal contraceptive effectiveness.
Use public-health TB follow-up when required.
medicationSafety: Numerous interactions occur through enzyme induction.
Intermittent or inconsistent therapy can increase adverse immunologic reactions and resistance risk.
redFlags: Clinical failure of a critical interacting medication
teaching: Orange secretions are expected; report jaundice, severe rash, bleeding, or pregnancy risk concerns.
delegationScope: Interaction assessment and TB regimen changes require licensed/provider review; adherence support can be shared under protocol.
examTrap: Labeling orange urine as hematuria or failing to review drug interactions.
oneLinePearl: Rifampin turns fluids orange and drug levels down.

title: Ethambutol: Vision Monitoring Matters
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Ethambutol can cause optic neuritis and color-vision changes. Baseline and ongoing visual assessment are important, and new blurred vision, reduced acuity, or red-green color discrimination change requires prompt escalation.
recognize: Toxicity may be bilateral and can involve reduced visual acuity, central scotoma, or color-vision disturbance.
Renal impairment can increase exposure because the drug is renally cleared.
priorities: Confirm baseline vision evaluation when part of the TB plan.
Ask about new visual symptoms at follow-up.
Report visual changes promptly before the next routine visit.
assessMonitor: Visual acuity/color discrimination per protocol, renal function, adherence, and TB treatment response.
interventions: Ensure eyeglasses/contact information and language-appropriate testing are available so baseline assessment is meaningful.
medicationSafety: Dose adjustment may be needed with renal impairment.
Do not dismiss visual complaints as age-related or fatigue during therapy.
teaching: Report blurred vision or color changes immediately.
Do not independently discontinue the rest of the TB regimen.
delegationScope: Routine symptom screening may be assisted, but interpretation of visual change and regimen decisions require licensed/provider escalation.
examTrap: Waiting until the next scheduled eye exam after a patient reports new blurred vision.
oneLinePearl: Ethambutol: if vision changes, act now.

title: Pyrazinamide: Liver and Uric Acid Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Pyrazinamide is part of initial multidrug TB therapy and can cause hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia. Monitor hepatic symptoms and report severe joint pain or gout-like symptoms while maintaining the prescribed regimen.
recognize: Anorexia, nausea, dark urine, jaundice, or unusual fatigue can indicate liver injury.
Uric acid may rise and can trigger gout symptoms in susceptible patients.
priorities: Review liver disease/alcohol exposure and gout history.
Monitor for hepatitis symptoms throughout the intensive phase.
Reinforce adherence to the full TB combination.
assessMonitor: Liver tests when ordered, uric acid when clinically relevant, joint symptoms, adherence, and TB response.
interventions: Encourage adequate hydration when not contraindicated and coordinate gout management with the treatment team if symptoms occur.
medicationSafety: Concurrent hepatotoxic drugs/alcohol can increase risk.
Do not stop pyrazinamide alone without TB-team direction unless an emergency toxicity plan directs otherwise.
redFlags: Severe acute monoarthritis with inability to bear weight
teaching: Report liver symptoms and severe joint pain promptly; complete therapy exactly as directed.
delegationScope: Monitoring and regimen adjustments require licensed/provider review; adherence support can be delegated under protocol.
examTrap: Stopping all TB medications because of one elevated uric-acid value without clinical evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Pyrazinamide: watch liver and uric acid.

title: Acyclovir and Valacyclovir: Hydration and Renal Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Acyclovir-class antivirals suppress herpes viruses but can cause renal and neurotoxicity when exposure accumulates, especially with dehydration or kidney impairment. Maintain appropriate hydration and use renal-adjusted dosing when prescribed.
recognize: Rising creatinine, reduced urine output, confusion, tremor, hallucinations, or lethargy can signal toxicity.
Early antiviral treatment is most effective in many herpes presentations.
priorities: Check renal function and hydration status before significant therapy.
Report abrupt confusion or kidney-function change.
Use IV infusion parameters exactly when IV acyclovir is ordered.
assessMonitor: Creatinine/eGFR, intake/output, hydration, mental status, lesion response, and infusion-site status for IV therapy.
interventions: Encourage fluids when clinically appropriate and not restricted.
Use lesion precautions and patient teaching appropriate to the infection.
medicationSafety: Dose reduction is commonly required with renal impairment.
Other nephrotoxic drugs can increase kidney risk.
teaching: Antivirals suppress outbreaks but do not eradicate latent herpes infection.
Maintain hydration as directed and report reduced urination or confusion.
delegationScope: Medication administration follows local scope; acute renal or neurologic change requires licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Continuing an unchanged dose despite major renal deterioration.
oneLinePearl: Acyclovir loves water and kidney-adjusted dosing.

title: Oseltamivir: Early Influenza Antiviral Therapy
bottomLine: Oseltamivir inhibits influenza neuraminidase and works best when started early, but high-risk or severely ill patients may still benefit when treatment begins later. It does not replace annual influenza vaccination.
recognize: Nausea and vomiting are common adverse effects.
Rare serious skin or neuropsychiatric reactions require prompt evaluation.
priorities: Start promptly when ordered for suspected or confirmed influenza in appropriate patients.
Adjust for renal impairment when prescribed.
Monitor hydration and clinical deterioration.
assessMonitor: Fever/respiratory symptoms, hydration, renal function when relevant, neurologic/behavioral changes, and response to therapy.
interventions: Administer with food if GI upset occurs and compatible with product instructions.
medicationSafety: Oseltamivir treats influenza, not bacterial pneumonia or non-influenza viral illness.
Vaccination remains the primary preventive strategy.
teaching: Complete the prescribed course and seek care for worsening breathing or confusion.
Antiviral therapy does not eliminate the need for vaccination.
delegationScope: Routine administration can follow local scope; worsening respiratory or neurologic status requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Withholding ordered treatment solely because symptom onset was more than 48 hours ago in a severely ill or high-risk patient.
oneLinePearl: Influenza antivirals are best early, but severity and risk still matter later.

title: Fluconazole: Liver, QT, and Interaction Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Fluconazole treats susceptible fungal infections but can cause hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, and clinically important drug interactions. Renal function affects dosing for repeated systemic therapy.
recognize: Jaundice, dark urine, severe fatigue, or persistent nausea may indicate liver injury.
Palpitations or syncope can indicate a clinically important rhythm disturbance in susceptible patients.
priorities: Review interacting medications and QT-risk factors.
Monitor liver symptoms and renal function when indicated.
Escalate severe rash or rhythm symptoms.
assessMonitor: Liver tests when ordered, renal function, electrolytes/QT risk in selected patients, infection response, and interacting drug effects.
interventions: Correct modifiable electrolyte abnormalities when ordered and relevant to QT risk.
medicationSafety: Fluconazole inhibits drug-metabolizing enzymes and can increase concentrations of interacting medications.
Pregnancy risks vary by dose/duration and indication and require clinician-specific decision-making.
teaching: Report jaundice, severe rash, or fainting/palpitations and disclose all medications.
delegationScope: Interaction assessment and abnormal hepatic/rhythm findings require licensed/provider review.
examTrap: Assuming an oral antifungal has no meaningful systemic interactions.
oneLinePearl: Fluconazole: fungi down, but watch liver, QT, and interactions.

title: Amphotericin B: Kidney and Electrolyte Toxicity
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Systemic amphotericin B can be lifesaving for severe fungal disease but is strongly associated with infusion reactions, nephrotoxicity, potassium/magnesium loss, and anemia. Renal and electrolyte monitoring is central to safe therapy.
recognize: Fever, chills, rigors, nausea, and hypotension may occur during infusion.
Rising creatinine, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, weakness, or dysrhythmia can indicate significant toxicity.
priorities: Verify baseline renal function/electrolytes and ordered premedication/hydration plan.
Monitor closely during infusion.
Report kidney decline, severe hypotension, or dysrhythmia immediately.
assessMonitor: Creatinine, potassium, magnesium, CBC, vital signs during infusion, intake/output, and infusion-site status.
interventions: Use prescribed infusion duration and formulation-specific administration procedures.
Replace electrolytes only according to orders and current laboratory data.
medicationSafety: Different amphotericin formulations are not dose-for-dose interchangeable.
Concurrent nephrotoxins increase kidney risk.
teaching: Explain why frequent blood tests are needed and report reduced urine output, severe weakness, or palpitations.
delegationScope: IV administration and reaction management follow state/facility scope; acute toxicity requires licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Treating a stable infusion reaction and true anaphylaxis as the same event—or ignoring electrolyte loss because the infection is improving.
oneLinePearl: Amphotericin B saves lives but taxes kidneys and electrolytes.

title: Clindamycin: C. difficile Risk Is the Exam Pearl
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Clindamycin is useful for selected susceptible infections but carries a major risk of C. difficile-associated diarrhea. New significant diarrhea during or after therapy requires evaluation rather than reflex antidiarrheal treatment.
recognize: Watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, fever, leukocytosis, dehydration, or severe abdominal distention can signal C. difficile infection.
C. difficile disease can occur after the antibiotic course ends.
priorities: Ask about stool frequency and severity when diarrhea occurs.
Institute C. difficile precautions/testing pathway when clinically indicated.
Escalate severe abdominal findings, dehydration, or systemic toxicity.
assessMonitor: Stool pattern, hydration, electrolytes when indicated, abdominal findings, infection response, and allergy symptoms.
interventions: Avoid unnecessary antimotility agents unless specifically ordered after evaluation.
medicationSafety: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea can represent serious C. difficile colitis.
Complete therapy as prescribed unless the treating clinician changes the regimen.
teaching: Report persistent or severe diarrhea during or after therapy and do not self-treat with antidiarrheals without advice.
delegationScope: Routine administration may follow local scope; significant diarrhea or abdominal deterioration requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Giving loperamide automatically for severe antibiotic-associated diarrhea.
oneLinePearl: Clindamycin + new diarrhea = think C. difficile first.
